templates.title: Product page conversion by storefront and traffic source
templates.subtopic: first-event detection with ROW_NUMBER, last-touch attribution with LATERAL, distinct denominators

sections.scenario: An app marketplace shows developers how well each app's product page converts: of the people who viewed the page, how many downloaded the app for the first time. Developers break the number down by storefront (the country or region store) and by traffic source: search, browse, a referring app or a referring website. Re-downloads, where someone reinstalls an app they already had, are not new customers and must not inflate the rate. You are writing the query behind the report.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns app_id, storefront, source, viewers, downloads, conversion_rate, ordered by app_id, storefront, source. viewers is the number of distinct account_ids with at least one page_views row for that app, storefront and source. A download is a first-time download if it is the account's earliest download of the app (earliest downloaded_at, then lowest download_id); every other download is a re-download and is ignored. A first-time download is credited to the source of the account's last view of that app's page in the download's storefront at or before downloaded_at (latest viewed_at, then highest view_id); a first-time download with no such view is unattributed and counts nowhere. downloads counts the first-time downloads credited to the group, and conversion_rate = downloads / viewers, rounded to 4 decimal places. {{window_rule}} {{redownload_rule}} {{floor_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Groups with viewers but no credited downloads appear with 0 downloads. A view in the same second as the download is "at or before" it. The sample has {{views}} page views and {{downloads}} downloads.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical apps, accounts, storefront codes and traffic. The attribution rule is this exercise's simplification, not how any store's analytics attributes downloads. Accounts are pseudonymous identifiers; viewers who are not signed in are out of scope.
sections.criteria: First-time downloads detected across storefronts with a deterministic tie-break; one credited view per download, the last at or before it in the same storefront; the attribution window inclusive (Hard+); distinct viewers as the denominator with zero rows kept; duplicate download rows collapsed, the view tie broken by view_id and the floor applied (Very Hard); correct rounding and order; can discuss date attribution, alternative credit models, signed-out viewers and scale.

clarifications.q: Someone viewed the page from search, later from a referring website, then downloaded. Which source gets the download?
clarifications.a: The website: the last view at or before the download.

clarifications.q: Does a re-download after deleting the app count?
clarifications.a: No. Only the account's first download of the app counts, ever.

clarifications.q: A first-time download has no earlier view of the page in its storefront.
clarifications.a: It is unattributed and counts in no group. The account can still be a viewer.

clarifications.q: An account viewed the page only after downloading. Is it a viewer?
clarifications.a: Yes. viewers counts every distinct account that viewed the page from that source.

clarifications.q: How is the rate rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 4) of downloads over viewers, half away from zero.

hints: Find first-time downloads with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY account_id, app_id ORDER BY downloaded_at, download_id). Think about what adding storefront to that partition would do.
For each first-time download pick exactly one view: a LATERAL subquery with ORDER BY viewed_at DESC, view_id DESC LIMIT 1, or DISTINCT ON over the joined candidates.
Build the denominator on its own (distinct accounts per app, storefront and source) and LEFT JOIN the credited downloads onto it, so groups without downloads survive.
followups: Developers want the rate by day. Does a conversion belong to the day of the view or of the download, and what happens to a view on Monday that converts on Tuesday?
Last-view attribution gives all the credit to the final touch. How would you report a first-touch view alongside it, and how would you explain to a developer why the two disagree?
Many viewers are not signed in. How would you estimate their conversion without linking identities, and what minimum count would you require before showing a small storefront's rate?
At billions of page views a day, how would you find the credited view for each download without a join that touches every view?

rules.ask: An account downloaded the app in one storefront and later in another. Is the second download a first-time download in your query?
An account viewed the page three times from search. How many viewers is that in your denominator?
The rule credits the last view before the download. Which source does your query credit for someone who found the app in search and came back from a website?
Where in your result does a source with viewers but no downloads go?
A view and the download happen in the same second. Does your condition credit that view, and should it?

templates.title: Billing retry recovery within N days, grace period included
templates.subtopic: episodes from an event stream with a running-sum split, inclusive interval windows

sections.scenario: When an auto-renewing subscription's renewal payment fails, an app store keeps retrying the payment for a while (billing retry). A developer can also offer a billing grace period, during which the subscriber keeps access while the store retries. A developer dashboard reports, per plan and storefront, how many subscriptions entered billing retry, how many recovered (renewed successfully) within {{n_days}} days, and how many of those recovered during the grace period. The retry and grace rules here are this exercise's; check current documentation for any real store's.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns plan_id, storefront, entered, recovered, recovered_in_grace, recovery_rate: one row per plan and storefront with at least one counted episode, ordered by plan_id, storefront. Read each subscription's billing_events in event_ts, event_id order. A renewal_failed event while the subscription is not already in billing retry opens an episode; further renewal_failed events while it is open are retry attempts. The episode closes at the next renewed event (it recovered then) or expired event (it did not). An episode is recovered if it closed with renewed at most {{n_days}} days after it opened: the {{n_days}} days count from the failed renewal that opened it, grace period included. It is recovered in grace if it is recovered, its plan's grace_days is greater than 0, and the renewal came at most grace_days days after it opened. entered counts episodes; recovery_rate = recovered / entered, rounded to 4 decimal places. {{episode_rule}} {{plan_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Both windows are inclusive: exactly {{n_days}} days (or exactly grace_days days) after opening still counts. An episode still open in the data counts in entered and not as recovered. The tables are a snapshot taken at {{as_of}}. The sample has {{subs}} subscriptions and {{events}} billing events.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical plans, grace periods, storefronts and events. A day is 24 hours in UTC. Price increases, refunds, family sharing and voluntary cancellations are out of scope.
sections.criteria: Episodes opened only by the first failure and closed by the next renewal or expiry; the window counted from entering retry with the grace period inside it; inclusive boundaries on timestamps; ordinary renewals and renewals after expiry not counted as recoveries (Hard+); the episode's own plan and immature episodes left out (Very Hard); correct rounding and order; can discuss cohort maturity, measuring a grace-period change and late notifications.

clarifications.q: A renewal fails, fails again three days later, then succeeds. How many entries is that?
clarifications.a: One episode, recovered. The second failure is a retry attempt inside the open episode.

clarifications.q: Does the {{n_days}}-day window start when the grace period ends?
clarifications.a: No. It starts at the failed renewal that opened the episode; the grace period is inside it.

clarifications.q: A subscription renews {{n_days}} days and one second after entering retry.
clarifications.a: That renewal closes the episode, but it is not a recovery within {{n_days}} days.

clarifications.q: A plan has grace_days = 0.
clarifications.a: It has no grace period, so none of its recoveries are in grace.

clarifications.q: How is the rate rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 4) of recovered over entered, half away from zero.

hints: A running SUM(CASE WHEN event_type IN ('renewed', 'expired') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) over each subscription's events cuts its history into stretches, each ending at a closing event.
Within a stretch, the first renewal_failed opens the episode, and the episode's closing event is the one whose running count is one higher.
Compare timestamps with intervals (start_ts + make_interval(days => grace_days)), not dates, so that the boundaries are exact.
followups: The dashboard shows this by month of entry. Why does the most recent month always look worse, and how would you present it honestly?
A developer lengthens the grace period. How would you measure whether recoveries rose because of it rather than because of the season?
Billing events arrive as notifications, sometimes late and sometimes twice. How do you keep the episode table idempotent when an old renewed arrives after an expired?
How would you maintain episodes incrementally each day for hundreds of millions of subscriptions without rescanning every history?

rules.ask: The event after a failure is often another failure. How does your query find the event that actually closes the episode?
Where does your {{n_days}}-day window start, and why is the grace period not added on top of it?
A subscription expires, is bought again and renews. Does your query count that renewal as a recovery?
A renewal lands on the last day of the window but later in the day than the failure. Does comparing dates instead of timestamps change your answer?
A subscription entered billing retry twice in the period. How many entries does your count give it?
A subscriber changed plans after an episode. Which plan does your query give that earlier episode?

templates.title: Library adds within seven days of a listener's first listen, per genre
templates.subtopic: per-pair first events, exclusion before aggregation, bridge-table rollups with a distinct-count floor

sections.scenario: A music streaming service wants to know which genres turn first listens into saved music: of the tracks a listener hears for the first time, how many do they add to their library within a week? Tracks the listener had saved before ever listening (from a recommendation or a shared playlist) are not evidence of a listen converting, so they are left out. Small genres are hidden until enough different listeners are behind the number.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns genre, listeners, pairs, added, add_rate, ordered by add_rate descending, then genre. A pair is a listener and a track with at least one listen; its first listen is the earliest listen's played_at. {{listen_rule}} Take the listener's earliest library_adds row for that track: if it is before the first listen, the pair is left out entirely; if it is at or after the first listen and no more than 7 days later, the pair is added; otherwise (later, or never added) the pair counts as not added. Per genre, pairs counts the pairs of its tracks, added the added ones, listeners the distinct listeners among those pairs, and add_rate = added / pairs, rounded to 4 decimal places. Return only genres with at least {{min_listeners}} listeners. {{genre_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The window is inclusive at both ends: an add in the same second as the first listen counts, and so does one exactly 7 days (INTERVAL '7 days') later. Adds of tracks the listener never listened to are ignored. The sample has {{plays}} plays and {{adds}} library adds.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical listeners, tracks, genres and thresholds; the listen rule is this exercise's, not any service's royalty or reporting rule. Removals from the library are not logged; the earliest add is the one that decides.
sections.criteria: One row per pair from the earliest listen and earliest add; pre-added pairs excluded from both sides; inclusive 7-day window on timestamps; previews never starting the clock (Hard+); multi-genre tracks counted in each genre (Very Hard); a distinct-listener floor; correct rounding and ordering with the tie-break; can discuss album-level definitions, late offline plays, privacy floors and incremental computation.

clarifications.q: A listener saved a track from a playlist, then listened to it a day later.
clarifications.a: The pair is left out: the earliest add is before the first listen.

clarifications.q: A track was added within the week, removed, and added again a month later.
clarifications.a: Added. Only the earliest add matters.

clarifications.q: Is the floor on listeners or on pairs?
clarifications.a: Distinct listeners. One listener with six tracks in a genre is one listener.

clarifications.q: An add exactly seven days after the first listen?
clarifications.a: It counts: added_at <= first_listen + INTERVAL '7 days'.

clarifications.q: How is the rate rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 4) of added over pairs, half away from zero. Equal rates are ordered by genre.

hints: Reduce to one row per pair first: the earliest listen and, separately, the earliest add, joined on (listener_id, track_id) with a LEFT JOIN.
Drop pre-added pairs before aggregating; they belong in neither the numerator nor the denominator.
Join pairs to track_genres last, and use COUNT(DISTINCT listener_id) for the floor.
followups: Product wants the same metric for albums. What is the pair, and what is a "first listen" of an album?
Plays from an offline device sync days later. What does that do to the first listen and the window, and how would you keep a published number stable?
Is a listener floor enough to protect privacy for a niche genre in a small storefront? What else would you add?
At billions of plays a day, how would you keep each pair's first listen and earliest add up to date without rescanning history?

rules.ask: A listener added a track within the week, removed it and added it again a month later. Which add does your query look at?
Your floor counts rows. How many listeners does a genre have if one person played six of its tracks?
An add happens exactly seven days after the first listen, to the second. Does your comparison count it?
Where does a pair whose track was saved before it was ever played drop out of your query, and does it leave the denominator too?
A short preview came first and the real listen a day later. Which one starts your seven-day clock?
A track belongs to two genres. How many times does its pair count, and what happens if someone sums your rows into an overall rate?

templates.title: Time-synced lyrics: the line on screen at each playback position
templates.subtopic: sort once and binary search, half-open intervals, stable original indexes

sections.scenario: A music app shows lyrics line by line in time with the song. Each line has a start and an end time; during an instrumental break no line is highlighted. Listeners scrub, jump back to replay a chorus and skip ahead, so the app must find the line for any position quickly, not just the next one. The same lookup runs in batch over sampled playback positions to check lyric timing quality.
sections.problem: Implement current_lines(lines, positions, duration_ms=None). lines is a list of (start_ms, end_ms) with 0 <= start_ms < end_ms; a line is on screen at position p when start_ms <= p < end_ms. {{order_rule}} Apart from corrections that share a start, lines never overlap. positions is a list of non-negative integers in the order they were sampled; each can be anywhere relative to the one before (seeks and replays). {{repeat_rule}} Return a list with, for each position, the index in lines of the line on screen, or -1 when no line is.
sections.constraints: Up to 50 000 lines (a long live recording with a synced transcript) and 200 000 positions. Seeks are frequent, so the work per position must not grow with the number of lines.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical timings. Word-level timing and translations exist in real lyric formats and are out of scope.
sections.criteria: Half-open intervals with gaps returning -1; one sort and a binary search per position rather than a scan or a resettable pointer; original indexes preserved; corrections with the same start resolved by the last listing (Hard+); repeat-one positions wrapped (Very Hard); empty inputs handled; a clear complexity argument; credible discussion of the playback fast path, overlapping lines and batch timing checks.

clarifications.q: A position equals a line's end.
clarifications.a: That line is no longer on screen. If another line starts exactly there, it is; otherwise -1.

clarifications.q: Can positions go backwards?
clarifications.a: Yes, at any time: a listener replays a chorus or scrubs back to the start.

clarifications.q: What if lines is empty?
clarifications.a: Every position gets -1, and no positions gives [].

clarifications.q: Do I return the line's text?
clarifications.a: No: the index into lines exactly as given.

clarifications.q: Can two lines share a start?
clarifications.a: Only where this round says so; then the one listed later replaces the earlier one completely.

hints: For any position, the only candidate is the line with the largest start at or before it; then check that the position is before that line's end.
Sort the starts once, keeping each line's original index, and use bisect.bisect_right(starts, p) - 1.
Resolve duplicate starts before sorting: a dict from start to index, filled in input order, keeps the last listing.
followups: On a device, positions arrive many times a second during normal play. How would you make the common case O(1) while keeping a seek O(log n)?
In a duet, two singers' lines can be on screen at once. What structure returns every line covering a position, and at what cost?
A listener sets a sync offset of +300 ms for one song. Where do you apply it so that every boundary stays exact?
A batch job checks lyric timing against the audio for millions of songs. How would you distribute it, and what would you measure to flag a badly synced file?

rules.ask: How many line checks does your solution make for 200 000 positions over 50 000 lines?
What does your pointer do when the listener seeks back to the start of the song every few seconds?
Do you use bisect_left or bisect_right, and what does each give for a position exactly at a line's start?
After sorting, how do you return the line's index in the original list, and which of two lines with the same start do you keep?
What is on screen at a position exactly equal to duration_ms?

templates.title: Subscription renewal dates with upgrades and downgrades
templates.subtopic: month-index math with clamping, event ordering, O(1) jumps instead of simulation

sections.scenario: An app store sells auto-renewing subscriptions in plans of different service levels and lengths. A subscription renews on the same day of the month it was bought: one bought on 31 January renews on the last day of February, then on 31 March. Subscribers move between plans: in this exercise an upgrade takes effect at once and starts a new period, while a downgrade waits until the next renewal. These rules are this exercise's, loosely modelled on public descriptions of subscription upgrades and downgrades; check current documentation for any real store. Finance needs, for every subscription, the next renewal date and the plan that will renew on it.
sections.problem: Implement renewals(plans, subs, as_of). plans maps a plan name to (tier, months): a higher tier is a higher service level (no two plans share a tier) and months is the plan's period length. Each element of subs is (purchase_date, plan, changes), where changes is a list of (date, new_plan) in date order; all dates are 'YYYY-MM-DD' strings. A subscription has an anchor day and a period start, both taken from the purchase date at first. Its renewals fall months, 2 × months, … months after the period start, each on the anchor day or, in a shorter month, on that month's last day. A change to a plan with a higher tier than the plan in effect is an upgrade: the new plan is in effect from the change date, which becomes the new period start and anchor day. A change to a lower tier is a downgrade: it is pending until the first renewal strictly after the change date; at that renewal the new plan renews, and the next period (of the new plan's length) starts there, with the same anchor day. {{pending_rule}} {{change_rule}} Return a list with one entry per subscription: (date, plan), the first renewal strictly after as_of and the plan that renews on it.
sections.constraints: Up to 150 000 subscriptions with a few changes each. The stress test uses synthetic purchase dates going back decades, so the work per subscription must not grow with the number of periods that have passed.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical plans and tiers. Prices, proration, refunds, free trials and billing retry are out of scope. Dates are calendar dates with no time zone.
sections.criteria: Renewals anchored to the original day and clamped per month, never drifting; the first renewal strictly after as_of; upgrades re-anchoring immediately and downgrades taking effect at the next renewal (Hard+); pending downgrades cancelled or replaced correctly and renewals ordered before same-day changes (Very Hard); None for future purchases and future changes ignored; O(1) work per subscription plus O(1) per change; credible discussion of proration, materialising future renewals and time zones.

clarifications.q: Bought on 31 January on a monthly plan. When does it renew?
clarifications.a: 28 February (29 in a leap year), then 31 March, 30 April, 31 May: the anchor stays 31, only the month's length clamps it.

clarifications.q: A renewal falls exactly on as_of.
clarifications.a: It is not after as_of; return the one after it.

clarifications.q: An upgrade on 30 April from a plan anchored on the 31st.
clarifications.a: The upgrade re-anchors: from then on the anchor day is 30.

clarifications.q: A downgrade requested on a renewal day.
clarifications.a: That day's renewal has already happened, so the downgrade waits for the next one.

clarifications.q: A subscription bought on as_of itself.
clarifications.a: Its first renewal, one period after the purchase.

hints: Work in month indexes (year * 12 + month - 1). Renewal k falls in month start + k × months, on min(anchor_day, days_in_month).
The first renewal after a date t is renewal k = max(1, (month_index(t) - start) // months) or the one after it; check which.
Between changes nothing happens except renewals, so the schedule only needs evaluating at each change date and at as_of.
followups: Finance wants every renewal in the next 90 days for all subscriptions, one row each. How would you generate them without stepping from the purchase date?
Suppose an upgrade refunds the unused part of the old period. How would you compute that proration, and which day count would you agree with finance?
Someone stores only the last renewal date and computes the next as "last renewal plus one month". What goes wrong, and when?
Subscribers in different time zones see the renewal on different local dates. Which time zone should the anchor live in, and what changes in this function?

rules.ask: A monthly plan bought on 31 January: does adding 30 days give the right renewal in February, and in March?
Adding one month at a time to the previous renewal turns 31 January into 28 February and then 28 March. Where does your code keep the original anchor day?
How many iterations does your loop make for a monthly subscription bought decades before as_of, across 150 000 subscriptions?
How does your clamp handle 29 February on an annual plan in a non-leap year, and does the next leap year get the 29th back?
A downgrade is pending and the subscriber upgrades before it takes effect. What happens to the pending downgrade in your code?

templates.title: Grouping near-duplicate photos by perceptual hash
templates.subtopic: Hamming-distance search with the pigeonhole principle, union-find

sections.scenario: A photo library that syncs across a person's devices offers to tidy up near-duplicate shots: bursts, re-saved edits, the same scene taken twice. In this exercise each photo has a 64-bit perceptual hash, computed on the device from a small downscaled copy of the image, so that photos that look alike get hashes that differ in only a few bits. The grouping also runs on the device, over libraries of tens of thousands of photos, so it has to be fast and must not compare every pair.
sections.problem: Implement group_near_duplicates(photos, max_bits, keep_best=False). photos is a list of (photo_id, phash, score): a string id, a 64-bit hash given as an integer from 0 to 2⁶⁴ − 1, and an integer quality score. Two photos are near duplicates when their hashes differ in at most max_bits bit positions (their Hamming distance). Near duplicates chain: if A is a near duplicate of B and B of C, all three are one group, even when A and C differ in more bits. Return every group of two or more photos as a list of photo ids, and list the groups in order of the smallest photo id each contains (ids compare as plain strings). A photo with no near duplicate is in no group, and an empty library returns []. {{input_rule}} {{keep_rule}} The examples use max_bits = {{max_bits}}.
sections.constraints: Up to 40 000 photos in the timing check, with max_bits up to 4 there and at most 8 anywhere. All 64 bits of a hash are used. Comparing every pair is 800 million comparisons at that size and is far too slow. Aim for bucket work close to O(n · (max_bits + 1)) plus the pairs that land in the same bucket.
sections.assumptions: Hashes, scores and photo ids are hypothetical. How any real photo app computes hashes or finds duplicates is out of scope: this is an exercise in the technique. All photos belong to one person's library and are processed on their own device.
sections.criteria: Correct groups under chaining with inclusive max_bits; all 64 bits handled; empty and single-photo cases; exclusion of photos without a hash and one entry per repeated photo (Hard); keeper chosen by score with the smaller id on a tie, groups still ordered by their smallest id (Very Hard); the pigeonhole multi-index stated and justified before coding; union-find or an equivalent linear merge; a clear cost argument in terms of n, max_bits and bucket sizes; sensible answers on larger max_bits, incremental updates and distribution.

clarifications.q: Is "near duplicate" transitive?
clarifications.a: The grouping is. A group is a set of photos connected by near-duplicate pairs, so A and C can share a group through B even when they are far apart.

clarifications.q: Is max_bits inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes. Hashes that differ in exactly max_bits bits are near duplicates.

clarifications.q: Can two different photos have identical hashes?
clarifications.a: Yes, for example a photo and an exact copy. They differ in 0 bits.

clarifications.q: Can I assume a hash fits in 63 bits?
clarifications.a: No. The highest bit is used like any other.

clarifications.q: What order do I return?
clarifications.a: Groups ordered by the smallest photo id they contain. Inside a group, ids ascend, unless keep_best asks for the keeper first.

hints: If two 64-bit hashes differ in at most d bits, cut both into d + 1 blocks of bits. At most d blocks can hold a difference, so at least one block is identical in both.
For each block position, bucket the photos by that block's value. Only photos that share a bucket can be near duplicates, and only those need an exact bit count.
Merge confirmed pairs with union-find, and skip a pair whose photos are already in the same set.
followups: max_bits grows to 12. What happens to your block widths and bucket sizes, and what would you change?
A library holds 500 000 photos and gains a few dozen a day. How do you keep the groups current without regrouping everything?
A slow pan becomes one huge chained group. How would you change the grouping so that every member is close to one representative photo, and what does that cost?
A music catalogue wants the same check over a billion pieces of cover artwork in a batch pipeline. How do you distribute it, and what does the pigeonhole trick become?

rules.ask: How many comparisons is that for 40 000 photos, and how long does CPython take to do them?
Two hashes that differ only in the highest bit are far apart in sorted order. What does a sort by hash miss, and how would several sorts with permuted bits help?
How does a BK-tree's search cost grow with max_bits on uniformly spread 64-bit hashes, compared with your buckets?
A burst of 30 000 near-identical shots forms one long chain. What happens to a recursive search on it in Python?
What do path compression and union by rank each buy you here, and does the order of unions change the groups you return?

templates.title: Content-defined chunks for an app update delta
templates.subtopic: rolling hash, content-defined chunking, deduplication

sections.scenario: When a developer publishes a new version of an app, devices that already have the previous version should download only what changed. A technique that file-sync and backup tools use is content-defined chunking: cut a file wherever a rolling hash of the last few bytes matches a pattern. An insertion near the start of a file then changes only the chunks around it, and the later boundaries are found again. In this exercise the device chunks the files it has installed, the update is chunked the same way, and the device downloads only the chunks it does not already have.
sections.problem: Implement delta_chunks(installed, new, window, mask_bits, min_size=1, max_size=None). installed is a list of bytes, the files already on the device, and new is the bytes of the new version. For a file b, the window hash at position i is defined only when i ≥ window − 1: H(i) = (b[i − window + 1]·257^(window − 1) + … + b[i − 1]·257 + b[i]) mod 1 000 000 007. Cut each file into chunks from left to right. A chunk ends after byte i when the low mask_bits bits of H(i) are all zero, that is H(i) mod 2^mask_bits = 0. {{size_rule}} The bytes after the last cut form the final chunk. The window always covers the window bytes that end at i in the whole file, so it may reach back into the previous chunk. Every installed file is cut by the same rule. Then walk the chunks of new in order. A chunk must be downloaded unless the device already has a chunk with exactly the same bytes, either from an installed file or because an earlier chunk of new was downloaded. Return (chunk_count, downloads): the number of chunks in new, and the (offset, length) of each chunk to download, in file order, with offsets into new. An empty new returns (0, []). {{files_rule}}
sections.constraints: About 2 MB is hashed in the timing check with a 64-byte window, so recomputing every window from scratch, O(n · window), is too slow. One constant-time update per byte is expected. 1 ≤ window ≤ 64, 1 ≤ mask_bits ≤ 20, min_size ≥ 1, and max_size ≥ min_size when given.
sections.assumptions: The hash constants, sizes and files are hypothetical, chosen for this exercise. Chunks are compared by their bytes; a production system would compare a strong digest of each chunk. How any real app store packages or delivers updates is out of scope.
sections.criteria: Exact H(i) and boundaries from the first full window; the window running over the whole file, not restarting per chunk; min_size and max_size applied as specified (Hard); chunks compared by content across several installed files and repeats inside the update (Very Hard); empty and short files; a rolling update in O(1) per byte with the outgoing weight precomputed; a clear complexity argument; insight into why content-defined chunking resynchronises and how its parameters trade chunk count against reuse.

clarifications.q: Does the window restart at each chunk boundary?
clarifications.a: No. H(i) always covers the window bytes ending at i in the whole file. Only the size limits look at the current chunk.

clarifications.q: Is a chunk that appears twice in new downloaded twice?
clarifications.a: No. Once it is downloaded, the device has it.

clarifications.q: Are offsets into new or into the installed file?
clarifications.a: Into new. The device fetches the bytes at that offset and length from the new version.

clarifications.q: May I use a set of bytes, or hashlib, to compare chunks?
clarifications.a: Yes, either, for chunk identity. The boundary test must use exactly H(i) as defined.

clarifications.q: What if the file is shorter than the window?
clarifications.a: No hash is defined, so only max_size can cut it. Usually it is a single chunk.

hints: Write H(i) in terms of H(i − 1): take away the byte that leaves the window times 257^(window − 1), multiply by 257, and add the new byte, all modulo the prime.
Compute 257^(window − 1) mod 1 000 000 007 once, with pow(257, window - 1, MOD). In Python, % keeps the result non-negative after the subtraction.
Cut the installed files first and keep their chunks in a set. Then walk new once.
followups: Why do content-defined boundaries survive an insertion near the start when fixed-size blocks do not? What does one inserted byte cost each scheme?
What does mask_bits control? How would you choose it, min_size and max_size for a 2 GB game whose updates touch 200 MB?
The update service answers millions of devices on many older versions. What would it precompute per version, and what would a device send to ask for its delta?
Compressed or encrypted files change completely after a one-byte edit. What does that do to chunk reuse, and what would you change in how the app package is built?

rules.ask: How many byte operations is recomputing each window for 2 MB with a 64-byte window, and how long does CPython take for that?
int.from_bytes gives a base-256 value. Is that the hash this exercise defines, and what would change if it were?
Insert one byte at offset 10 of a file cut into fixed 4 KB blocks. How many blocks change, and how many would change with your chunks?
You identify chunks with a cryptographic digest. Why is that fine for identity but far too slow for the per-byte boundary test?
After the outgoing byte is subtracted the value can be negative. What does Python's % do with it, and what would C or Java do?

templates.title: Debug the developer proceeds report
templates.subtopic: tax-inclusive prices, commission tiers, rounding, refunds, currency keys

sections.scenario: An app store pays developers their proceeds: what the customer paid, minus any tax included in the price, minus the store's commission. In this exercise the commission is 30%, reduced to 15% for a subscription once the subscriber has had a year of paid service (this exercise's rule; check current docs). Prices in some storefronts include tax, and developers are paid separately in each currency. Developers have raised several complaints about one report. Proceeds in storefronts whose prices include VAT look too low. A renewal on the exact anniversary of a subscriber's first purchase is charged the full rate. Some sales show proceeds one minor unit higher than the developer's own calculation. A refund that arrives just after the first year takes back more than the sale paid. And sales from two storefronts that use the same currency appear as two rows. The report below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix proceeds_report(transactions) so that it meets this specification. transactions is a list of dicts in date order (ISO dates YYYY-MM-DD, and a refund always comes after its sale). {{replay_rule}}

  1. sale {"type", "txn", "app", "product", "subscriber", "storefront", "currency", "price", "tax_bp", "date"}. price is what the customer paid, in integer minor units of currency, including tax at tax_bp basis points (0 means no tax is included). The net price is price × 10000 / (10000 + tax_bp), rounded half up to a whole minor unit.
  2. Rate. The commission rate is 15% when the sale's date is 365 or more days after the earliest sale of the same product to the same subscriber, and 30% otherwise. Days are calendar days between the two dates, and breaks in service are ignored in this exercise.
  3. Proceeds. The commission is net × rate / 100, rounded half up to a whole minor unit, and the proceeds are net − commission.
  4. refund {"type", "txn", "original", "date"} reverses the original sale exactly: one unit and that sale's proceeds are taken off the sale's row. A refund of an unknown sale, or of a sale already refunded, changes nothing. A refunded sale still counts as the subscriber's first sale.
  5. Output. One row [app, currency, units, proceeds] per app and currency, combining every storefront that uses that currency. units is sales minus refunds applied. Rows are sorted by app, then currency.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 200 000 transactions, processed in linear time. Integer arithmetic only.
sections.assumptions: Prices, tax rates, storefronts, apps and the commission rule are hypothetical and simplified; check current docs for any real store's terms. There is no currency conversion: each currency is paid on its own. The tax rate is given on each transaction.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its business symptom; divides tax out of a tax-inclusive price; starts the reduced rate on day 365; rounds half up with integer arithmetic, not round(); reverses a refund from the stored sale; groups rows by app and currency; keeps the fix minimal and linear; adds a test per bug.

clarifications.q: Is the price before or after tax?
clarifications.a: After: it already includes the tax. Divide the tax out; do not subtract a percentage of the price.

clarifications.q: Does the 365th day count?
clarifications.a: Yes. A sale 365 or more days after the first one earns the 15% rate.

clarifications.q: How is half a minor unit rounded?
clarifications.a: Up, for both the net price and the commission. Every value is non-negative before refunds are applied.

clarifications.q: Which rate does a refund use?
clarifications.a: None of its own. A refund reverses exactly what the original sale paid.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Work a sale by hand: price 999 with tax_bp 1900. What is the net, and what does the code compute?
Compute 995 * 30 / 100 and pass it to round(). What does Python do with an exact .5?
What should a refund take off the row, and what does the code take off when the refund is dated after the anniversary?
Two storefronts use the same currency. What key are the rows grouped by?
followups: Developers want one total in their own currency. Where would conversion happen, at which rate, and how do you keep last month's report reproducible?
A storefront's tax rate changes mid-month. What must each transaction carry so that any month's report can be rebuilt exactly?
A refund arrives two months after the sale, after that month's proceeds were paid. In which period do you report it, and how?
The rule changes so that a break in service longer than 60 days restarts the first year (this exercise's variant). What state would you keep per subscriber and product?

rules.ask: Python's decimal module rounds half to even by default too. Which rounding mode would you set, and where?
Where else in this report could a float creep in, and what would it do to a total over 200 000 transactions?
Which day's rate would you use for a refund dated after the month closed, and does the developer's statement agree?
Is "a year of paid service" 365 days or the same calendar date next year? What changes for a first purchase on 29 February?
Why is the storefront the wrong key for the payment rows, and what would you still report per storefront?

templates.title: Developer diagnostics from opted-in devices
templates.subtopic: privacy-conscious telemetry aggregation, crash grouping, mergeable percentiles

upload: once a day, when the device is charging and on Wi-Fi

sections.scenario: Device owners can choose to share diagnostics with app developers. In this exercise about {{devices}} opted-in devices record crashes, app launch times and battery impact for {{apps}} apps, summarise them on the device and upload {{upload}}. Developers see, per app version: crash rate, launch-time percentiles, battery use, and crash reports grouped into signatures. They see aggregates only: no device or person identifiers, and no number that fewer than {{min_devices}} devices contributed to.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline from on-device collection to the developer reports. Cover what the device records and summarises before upload and what it never sends; the upload format and which identifiers it carries; ingestion, duplicate uploads and late uploads; symbolication and grouping of crash reports into signatures; per app-version metrics (crash rate per device-day or per session, launch-time percentiles, battery impact); the release rule that enforces {{min_devices}} contributing devices; what happens when a person opts out; and how a developer sees a new version's metrics soon after release.
sections.constraints: No stable device identifier leaves the device in this exercise. Each upload is a daily report per device and app, with an identifier that is random for that report. Percentiles must be computed from summaries that merge, not from raw values. Crash reports contain memory addresses that become function names only with the symbol files the developer uploads, sometimes days later. A device that opts out stops uploading at once, and what it uploaded before must expire on a stated schedule.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, thresholds and schedules are hypothetical. The exercise describes a general technique for privacy-conscious aggregation; it does not describe how any platform builds its diagnostics or what any device records. A report carries the app, its version, the OS version, the device model family and the day.
sections.criteria: On-device summarisation that sends only what the reports need, with no stable identifiers; mergeable launch-time histograms and a defined crash-rate denominator; idempotent ingestion of re-sent and late reports; symbolication that can happen after arrival, with regrouping; signature grouping that is stable over time; a release rule enforced per published cell, including the subtraction problem; retention of raw reports separate from aggregates; a credible plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Can I count distinct devices behind a number without a device id?
clarifications.a: In this exercise each device sends at most one report per app per day, so reports per app, version and day count devices for that day. Counting distinct devices across days is not possible, by design.

clarifications.q: Do developers see individual crash reports?
clarifications.a: They see crash signatures with counts and a representative symbolicated stack. A stack is shown only when at least {{min_devices}} devices reported that signature.

clarifications.q: How fresh must the metrics be?
clarifications.a: A new version's first numbers within a day or two of release; earlier is better, as long as the release rule holds.

clarifications.q: Can a developer slice by device model and OS version?
clarifications.a: Yes, but every released cell must meet the release rule on its own.

clarifications.q: What happens to reports uploaded before an opt-out?
clarifications.a: They cannot be linked to the device, so they are not deleted one by one. They expire with the rest of that day's raw reports.

hints: Decide what the device summarises: a histogram of launch times with fixed bucket edges merges exactly by adding counts, while a list of raw values does not need to leave the device at all.
Apply the release rule at the cell you publish (app, version, model family, OS, day or week), after aggregation, and think about two overlapping cells that differ by a few devices.
Keep raw reports only as long as symbolication and reprocessing need them; keep the aggregates for the long run.
followups: A developer uploads symbols three days after a release. What do they see before that, and what do you reprocess when the symbols arrive?
Two released cells, "all models" and "all models except one", differ by three devices. What could someone learn by subtracting them, and how do you prevent it?
A new version reaches the {{min_devices}} threshold slowly because it is rolling out in phases. How do you show early numbers without breaking the release rule?
A crash signature splits into two after a compiler change, though it is the same bug. How do you keep the counts and trends continuous?

rules.ask: You keep a device identifier. What could a developer or an attacker learn from it, and how do you count devices for the release rule without it?
Launch times have a long tail. What does a mean hide, and how do you produce a p90 from millions of daily reports without their raw values?
A cell passes the threshold today, and a sibling cell with one device fewer is also released. How can comparing the two reveal one device, and what do you do?
Devices upload once a day. What would a streaming pipeline buy you here, and what would it cost?
Symbol files arrive after the crashes. What do you store so that you can group crashes before symbolication and regroup them after?

incidents: A popular app ships a version that crashes at launch on one device model family. Within a day, its crash reports are 30 times the usual volume, from about {{devices}} opted-in devices in total.
A developer reports that their crash rate for one version doubled overnight, but no new crash signature appeared, and that version's daily report count halved.

templates.title: Ratings and reviews with versions, resets and moderation
templates.subtopic: mutable user content, current state from events, recomputable aggregates

sections.scenario: An app store lets customers rate an app from 1 to 5 stars and, optionally, write a review, in {{storefronts}} storefronts. It receives about {{ratings_per_day}} ratings a day, and {{review_share}} comes with a written review. A customer has one current rating per app and storefront, and can change it or edit their review at any time. Developers can respond to reviews and edit their responses. Reviews can be reported and removed by moderation, and a removal can be reversed on appeal. In this exercise, a developer releasing a new version may reset the app's summary rating in a storefront (this exercise's rule; check current docs): the summary then counts only ratings submitted after the reset, while the written reviews stay visible. The product page shows each storefront's summary rating, updated {{freshness}}. Developers see ratings per app version, and how they changed over time.
sections.problem: Design the data model and pipeline for ratings and reviews. Cover the events (rating submitted or changed, review written, edited, removed or restored, response posted or edited, summary reset), the current-state tables they maintain, the storefront summary since the last reset, ratings per version, the history a developer can browse, how moderation decisions change the numbers, and how you rebuild everything from the events after a bug.
sections.constraints: A changed rating replaces the old one; it is never counted twice. In this exercise a rating whose review is removed by moderation stops counting in the summary until the review is restored. The summary must equal a recomputation from the events at any time. A reset must not change any rating or review, only what the summary counts. Customer identifiers must not appear in anything a developer sees.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, storefront counts and timings are hypothetical, and the moderation and reset rules are this exercise's. A rating event carries the customer, app, storefront, stars, the app version the customer had installed, and a timestamp.
sections.criteria: Current state per customer, app and storefront with ordered, idempotent updates; summaries as counts that change by subtraction and addition and equal a recomputation; resets as a filter, not a mutation; per-version attribution defined for changed ratings; moderation as reversible state with history; responses and edits versioned; a rebuild path from the events; customer identifiers kept from developers; a credible plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Which version does a rating belong to?
clarifications.a: The version installed when the rating was submitted or last changed. A changed rating moves to the version current at the change.

clarifications.q: After a reset, does a customer who rated before it count?
clarifications.a: Not in the summary, unless they change or resubmit their rating after the reset. Their review stays visible.

clarifications.q: How fast must a moderation removal affect the summary?
clarifications.a: Within the same {{freshness}} as any other change.

clarifications.q: Do developers see who rated?
clarifications.a: No. They see counts, distributions and the review text with a display name chosen by the customer.

clarifications.q: Can events arrive out of order?
clarifications.a: Yes, by a few seconds across regions. Each event carries a timestamp and a per-customer sequence number.

hints: Keep the summary as counts per star (or a sum and a count), not as an average, so that a change is a subtraction and an addition.
Make the current rating per customer, app and storefront the unit of truth, with the timestamp of its last change. A reset is then a timestamp that filters which current ratings count.
Treat a removal as a state on the review with history, never as a delete, because appeals restore it.
followups: A moderation batch removes 40 000 reviews in one storefront at once. Walk through what changes, in what order, and what the product page shows meanwhile.
A bug double-applied rating changes for six hours. How do you rebuild the summaries and the per-version numbers, and how do you prove they are right?
Developers want to know whether a version improved ratings. Which numbers would you give them, and how do you keep rating changes from one version leaking into another?
A storefront's rules require removing a customer's data when they close their account. What happens to their rating, their review, the developer's response and the summaries?

rules.ask: You store an average. How do you apply a change from 5 stars to 2, and a moderation removal, without the full history?
A customer changes their rating three times. How does each consumer of your log avoid counting it three times?
A customer rated 5 on version 3.0 and changes it to 2 on version 3.2. Which version's numbers change, and how?
How do you keep that store's summary equal to a recomputation after a moderation batch and an appeal?
A removed review is restored after an appeal. What must your model have kept, and what does the summary do?

incidents: After a large release, ratings in one storefront arrive at ten times the usual rate for an hour, out of {{ratings_per_day}} a day, and the summary falls behind its {{freshness}} target.
A developer resets the summary rating in all {{storefronts}} storefronts at once, and an hour later customers report that the product page still shows the old rating in a few of them.

templates.title: Subscription groups — levels, upgrades, downgrades, crossgrades, offers and family sharing
templates.subtopic: subscription chains, billing periods versus entitlement, scheduled changes, offer eligibility, shared access

sections.scenario: A developer sells auto-renewable subscriptions through an app store to about {{subscribers}} active subscribers in {{storefronts}} storefronts. Its products sit in one subscription group ranked into {{levels}} levels of service (level 1 is the highest). This exercise's rules, modelled on public store documentation (check current docs): a customer has at most one active subscription in a group; an upgrade to a higher level takes effect immediately and the unused part of the current period is refunded pro rata; a downgrade takes effect at the next renewal date; a crossgrade to another product of the same level takes effect immediately when the durations match and at the next renewal otherwise. An introductory offer (a free trial, pay as you go, or pay up front) can be redeemed once per customer per group; promotional offers are for current or lapsed subscribers. The developer has turned on family sharing, so a purchaser's subscription also gives access to family members; about {{family_share}} of entitled users are family members, not purchasers. The developer learns about all of this from the store's server notifications and its own app accounts; in this exercise every notification carries a unique id, a signed date and an original transaction id that stays the same for a customer's chain in the group.
sections.problem: Design the data model the developer's data team builds from those notifications. Cover: the product catalogue (group, level, product, duration, price per storefront over time); the subscription chain per customer and group; billing periods (product, level, start, end, price, currency, offer applied) versus entitlement (what the customer could actually use at any instant); scheduled changes (a pending downgrade or crossgrade that is not yet effective); refunds and revocations; introductory and promotional offer redemptions and the eligibility decision for each; family-shared access. Then define the facts that answer "active paid subscribers by level and storefront per day", "trial-to-paid conversion by offer and storefront", "monthly moves between levels (upgrades, downgrades, crossgrades)", "family members versus purchasers" and "revenue per day by level", and say at which grain each lives.
sections.constraints: A chain's billing periods never overlap: at any instant a customer has at most one effective product in the group. A scheduled change is not effective until its date and can be cancelled before then. History must be reconstructable as it was known at any time. Money is integer minor units per currency; currencies are never added. Notifications arrive late, more than once and out of order. Any intro-offer eligibility decision can be explained from stored data.
sections.assumptions: Subscriber counts, levels, storefront counts and shares are hypothetical. The proration and offer rules are this exercise's, modelled on public documentation. Store commission and taxes are out of scope (another exercise covers proceeds). The developer sees only what the notifications and its own app accounts tell it; family members appear as their own entitlement records, marked as family-shared and linked to the purchaser's chain.
sections.criteria: Chain, periods and notifications kept apart; non-overlapping periods enforced; entitlement derived from periods and revocations; scheduled changes as their own records; upgrade, downgrade and crossgrade timing exactly as stated; proration as money events; eligibility per customer per group with replayable redemptions; family-shared access without revenue; facts at stated grains with a precise paid-subscriber definition; late and out-of-order notifications handled idempotently; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is a customer on a free trial a paid subscriber?
clarifications.a: No. Report trials separately; define "paid" precisely.

clarifications.q: What money moves on an upgrade in the middle of a month?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, the unused part of the old period is refunded pro rata and the new level is charged for a full period from the upgrade instant, which also becomes the new renewal date.

clarifications.q: Does a downgrade change today's access?
clarifications.a: No. It is scheduled: the customer keeps the higher level until the renewal date, and can cancel the scheduled change before then.

clarifications.q: Do family members count as subscribers?
clarifications.a: Your choice, but they never carry revenue and must be reportable separately from purchasers.

clarifications.q: What does a refund do to access?
clarifications.a: In this exercise a refund revokes access from the refund time and returns that period's money; access before the refund was real and stays in the history.

hints: Separate three things: the chain (customer × group, keyed by the original transaction id), the billing periods (one row per period with its product and price), and the raw notifications as received.
Entitlement is derived: at an instant, the period whose [start, end) contains it, cut short by any revocation. A scheduled change is its own record that becomes a period only when it takes effect.
Eligibility is per customer per group, not per product: keep redemptions so any decision can be replayed.
followups: Walk one customer: a free trial at level 3, converts to paid, upgrades to level 1 on day 10 of a monthly period, schedules a downgrade to level 2, renews. List the period rows, the scheduled-change row and every money movement.
Define "active paid subscribers by level on a date" precisely. A refund arrives 20 days after a period started: do you restate the past days' counts, and how is the report labelled?
Build the monthly level-move matrix. Does a crossgrade to a yearly product at the same level count as a move, and in which month: when it was chosen or when it took effect?
At {{subscribers}} subscribers, how do you build the daily active snapshot from the period table cheaply, and what does a notification that arrives three days late change?
The purchaser downgrades and later is refunded. What happens to each family member's access, to the "family members" count and to revenue per subscriber?

rules.ask: The customer upgraded on the 10th and scheduled a downgrade for the 28th. With one current-level column, what did they have on the 12th, and what will they have on the 28th?
Is a trial user a paid subscriber in your daily count? And can the same customer redeem another introductory offer on a different product in the same group?
Who is charged, who is entitled, and what happens to a family member's access when the purchaser is refunded?
A renewal notification arrives before the upgrade notification it follows. What do you store, and how does the period table end up right?
Where does the pro-rata refund live — on the old period, as a separate money event, or both — and how does revenue per day treat it?

incidents: Upgrade notifications delivered out of order created overlapping periods for some chains. Active subscribers summed over the {{levels}} levels exceeded total subscribers, and the overlap went unnoticed for a week.

Customers who crossgraded within the group were offered an introductory offer a second time because redemptions were keyed by product, not group. It happened across all {{storefronts}} storefronts before support noticed.
Revenue per subscriber dropped by about {{family_share}} the day family-shared entitlements were added to the subscriber denominator. Leadership read it as a pricing problem.

templates.title: Device lifecycle — activation, transfers, repairs, part replacements and trade-ins, as of a date
templates.subtopic: bitemporal intervals, serialised parts, ownership history, late records, data minimisation

sections.scenario: A device maker sells phones, tablets, laptops and watches in {{markets}} markets, with about {{devices}} devices in its records. Every device has a serial number. In this exercise: a device is activated by its first owner's account; it can change hands (sold, gifted, handed on in a company), and the next owner's activation starts a new ownership; it can be repaired by the maker or by independent and authorised repair providers, about {{repairs_per_day}} repairs a day, and a repair can replace parts (display, battery, camera, main board) that carry their own serials; a whole-unit replacement gives the customer a different device with a new serial and retires the old one; a trade-in returns the device for credit, after which it may be refurbished, with parts harvested or replaced, and sold again. Coverage plans attach to a device for a period. Records come from sales, activation, repair providers (whose records can arrive up to {{late_record_days}} days after the repair) and trade-in partners. Support, warranty, product quality and finance teams all ask "what was true about this device on a date".
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: device identity (serial, model, configuration) and the link between a retired serial and its replacement; ownership intervals; part installations as intervals per device and part slot; coverage intervals; the lifecycle events (activation, transfer, repair, replacement, trade-in, refurbishment, resale) and how they relate to the intervals; how a correction or a late record is stored so that both "what was true on the 5th" and "what did we know on the 5th" can be answered. Define the facts that answer "battery replacements per 1,000 devices by model and device age", "share of repairs done under coverage", "refurbished devices resold per month" and "devices in use per model per month", and say what an analyst may and may not see about owners.
sections.constraints: At any valid time a device has at most one owner and each part slot holds at most one part; a part serial is installed in at most one device at a time. Corrections never overwrite: they are new records with their own recorded time. Analysts never see owner identity, only a pseudonymous owner key that can be erased on request without breaking the device's history. Late records must not silently change a published monthly report.
sections.assumptions: Device counts, repair volumes, delays and market counts are hypothetical. The lifecycle rules are this exercise's. "In use" means activated and not retired, traded in or reported lost; it is not inferred from any device signal.
sections.criteria: Device identity separated from ownership, part and coverage intervals; bitemporal rows (valid and recorded time) so late records add rather than overwrite; non-overlap constraints per device, slot and part serial; events linked to the intervals they change; replacement serials linked; erasure that removes identity but keeps device history; facts with stated grains, denominators and a restatement policy; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is the owner the purchaser?
clarifications.a: Not necessarily: gifts, company-bought devices and second-hand sales all happen. Ownership here starts with an account's activation and ends with removal, transfer or trade-in.

clarifications.q: Can a part move from one device to another?
clarifications.a: Yes, during refurbishment a harvested part can be installed in another device. Its serial must not appear in two devices at once.

clarifications.q: A repair record arrives weeks late and says the battery was replaced on the 2nd. Which date counts?
clarifications.a: The repair happened on the 2nd (valid time). Reports produced before the record arrived did not know it (recorded time). You need both.

clarifications.q: Can an analyst look up who owned a device?
clarifications.a: No. Analysts see a pseudonymous owner key; support sees identity only within a customer case.

clarifications.q: What does a whole-unit replacement do to the history?
clarifications.a: The old serial is retired with a link to the new serial; the customer's coverage moves to the new device in this exercise.

hints: Keep the device (what it is) apart from intervals (who owned it, which part was in which slot, which coverage applied), each with valid_from and valid_to.
Add recorded_from and recorded_to to interval rows (bitemporal), so a late repair adds a row instead of rewriting one.
Events explain why an interval opened or closed; store them too, with keys from interval to event.
followups: Show the rows for one serial: activated by owner A, battery replaced, sold to owner B, display replaced under coverage, traded in, display harvested into another device, refurbished with a new display and sold to owner C.
A repair record arrives {{late_record_days}} days late. What changes in last month's battery replacement rate, and how do you publish the restated number next to the original?
A whole-unit replacement retires serial X and issues serial Y. How do "devices in use", device age and the customer's repair history connect across the two serials?
Owner B asks for their data to be erased. What is deleted, what is kept, and what does the device's history look like afterwards for owner C's warranty claim?
At {{devices}} devices with several serialised parts each, estimate the part-interval history and show how "which parts were in this device on a date" stays fast.

rules.ask: Owner B sold the device to owner C last month. With one owner column on the device row, who owned it when the display was replaced, and who sees that?
Is your valid_from the date the change happened or the date you learned about it? How do you reproduce last month's report exactly as published?
After erasure, how does the next owner's warranty claim still see that the device had a display replaced under coverage?
Support needs "parts in this device on the 3rd" in milliseconds. Do they replay every event, or is something materialised, and how is it kept equal to the log?
A whole-unit replacement issues a new serial for the same customer case, and a harvested part carries its own serial. Which keys does your model use for the device, the part and the case?

incidents: A repair provider's feed was down for {{late_record_days}} days. The weekly battery replacement rate for one model dipped, a quality review used the low number, and the backfill then raised it above the trend.
After a refurbishment batch, one display serial appears installed in two devices for overlapping periods: the harvest was recorded as an installation in the new device without closing the old one.

An erasure request deleted owner rows instead of the identity behind the pseudonymous key. The device's ownership intervals disappeared, and the next owner's coverage check failed in {{markets}} markets' support tools.

templates.title: Music catalogue identity — one recording on many releases, plays counted once
templates.subtopic: entity resolution, work–recording–release–track, many-to-many credits, cluster merges and restatement

sections.scenario: A music streaming service ingests catalogue deliveries from labels and distributors ({{sources}} sources here) into a catalogue of about {{catalogue_tracks}} tracks. A delivery describes a release (album, single, EP, compilation, deluxe edition, remaster) identified by a UPC, with its tracks; each track carries an ISRC identifying the recording, artist credits with roles (primary, featured, remixer), and, when known, the ISWC of the underlying musical work. The same recording appears on several releases: the single, the album, a compilation, a deluxe edition. In this exercise a remaster, a live version, a radio edit and the clean version of an explicit track are each a different recording. About {{dup_share}} of recordings arrive more than once from different sources with different identifiers or slightly different metadata, and occasionally two different audio files carry the same ISRC. Listeners play about {{daily_plays}} tracks a day. Charts, artist dashboards and the recommendation team all count plays: per recording, per "song" (all versions of a work by an artist), per release and per artist.
sections.problem: Design the catalogue and play model. Cover: the entities (work, recording, release, track as release × disc × position, artist, credit) and their keys; how source identifiers (ISRC, UPC, ISWC, each source's own ids) are stored and why they are or are not primary keys; deliveries, updates and takedowns as versions; the identity clusters that group duplicate recordings, and the separate grouping of versions into a song; how a cluster merge or split is recorded and applied. Then define the play fact (grain, keys, what it stores at play time) and how plays roll up to recording, song, release and artist without counting a play twice or splitting one recording's plays across duplicates. Say when a month's counts are final and how a later merge is handled.
sections.constraints: Each play is counted exactly once at each level of the hierarchy. A play keeps what was played (the track) even if the catalogue later changes. Cluster merges and splits are reversible and auditable. Artist reports for a closed month change only through a documented restatement. A takedown removes availability, not history.
sections.assumptions: Catalogue sizes, play volumes, source counts and duplicate shares are hypothetical. ISRC, UPC and ISWC are the public industry identifiers for recordings, releases and works; how any streaming service uses them internally is not part of this exercise. Royalty calculation is out of scope.
sections.criteria: Work, recording, release and track separated with internal keys; source identifiers kept as evidence, not primary keys; duplicate clusters and version-to-song grouping as versioned mappings; plays stored at track grain and rolled up through mappings so a play is counted once at each level; credit fan-out understood and fenced off; merges and splits reversible with an explicit restatement policy for published months; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is a remaster the same song?
clarifications.a: It is a different recording. Artist dashboards want song totals that include remasters and live versions; charts may want recordings. Define both levels.

clarifications.q: What does a play event identify?
clarifications.a: The track the listener played (a position on a release). The recording, song and artists are derived.

clarifications.q: Can an ISRC be wrong?
clarifications.a: Yes. Two different audio files can arrive with the same ISRC, and the same audio with two. Treat identifiers as evidence.

clarifications.q: How are plays split between a primary and a featured artist?
clarifications.a: For artist play counts, each credited artist gets the full play; for anything summed across artists you must not add those up as if they were plays. Say how your model prevents it.

clarifications.q: When is a month final?
clarifications.a: When its artist reports are published, a few days after month end.

hints: Mint internal ids for recordings, releases and works; keep source identifiers as attributes with their source and confidence.
Store the track id on the play. Map track → recording → cluster → song through mapping tables that are versioned in time, so a merge changes the mapping, not the play log.
Credits are many-to-many. Joining plays to credits multiplies rows: decide which metrics allow it (per-artist counts) and which must count distinct plays.
followups: Draw the rows for one song released as a single, on the album, on a compilation, and remastered on a deluxe edition. Ten plays are spread across the four. Give the counts per recording, per song and per release.
Two recordings from different sources are found to be duplicates and merged. What happens to last month's published artist report, and to this month's?
A track has one primary and two featured artists. What do the artist dashboards show, and what does a "total plays across all artists" query return?
At {{daily_plays}} plays a day, do you resolve the recording at ingestion, at query time, or both? How do you restate after a merge without rewriting the play log?
A distributor delivered a compilation whose tracks reuse the album's ISRCs but contain radio edits. How do you detect it, and how do you move the plays already counted?

rules.ask: Two different audio files arrive with the same ISRC from two sources. Which recording do plays of each belong to, and what does your key structure do with the collision?
After a merge of two recordings, last month's song totals change. Do you rewrite the published month, restate it, or only apply the merge going forward?
Your artist rollup joins plays to credits. What does the sum of plays over all artists equal now, and which reports must never use that sum?
Your play table stores the song and artist at write time. A cluster merge happens. How many rows do you rewrite, and how do you reproduce last month's numbers?
The same recording is on four releases. A chart wants the song's plays this week regardless of release. Which key do you group by, and where does it come from?

incidents: A batch of duplicate clusters (about {{dup_share}} of recordings) was merged mid-month. Artist dashboards for the previous, already published month changed overnight because the rollup read the current mapping.

A distributor's compilation reused the album's ISRCs for its radio edits. With {{sources}} sources delivering and no check of audio against identifiers, plays of the edits were counted as the album versions, and the song chart moved.
Artist-level totals summed in a label summary exceeded total plays by a third: featured-artist credits multiplied plays in a join, and the summary was published.

templates.title: App review submissions — builds, versions, decisions, resubmissions and time in review
templates.subtopic: workflow state history, review episodes, durations from transitions, rates with clear denominators

platforms: phone, tablet, desktop, TV and watch

sections.scenario: On an app store's developer platform, developers upload builds (each with a build number unique within its version), create an app version with a marketing version string, attach a build per platform and metadata (screenshots, description, privacy details), and submit it for review. This exercise's process, modelled on public developer documentation (check current docs): a submission waits for review, is in review, and ends approved (released at once or held for the developer to release), rejected with one or more guideline references and a message, rejected for metadata only (fixable without a new build), or removed by the developer. A developer can reply, fix and resubmit, upload a new build, or request an expedited review. A submission can carry several items (the app version, in-app purchases, in-app events). There are about {{submissions_per_week}} submissions a week across {{platforms}} platforms; about {{rejection_share}} of first submissions of a version are rejected and about {{expedite_share}} of submissions are expedited. The platform publishes review-time statistics, and each developer sees their own history.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: app, platform, version and build; the submission and its items; the state history of each submission; review episodes (one pass through review, from entering the queue to a decision) and their decisions; guideline citations; messages between developer and reviewer (stored as references, not analysed); resubmission links; expedite requests. Then define, with exact start and stop events, "time waiting", "time in review" and "time from first submission to approval" per version; "first-pass approval rate"; "rejections by guideline"; "resubmissions per approved version"; and the weekly percentile published as "most submissions are reviewed within N hours". Say which views a developer sees and which only the platform sees.
sections.constraints: State history is append-only with timestamps in UTC. A version can be submitted many times; each submission has exactly one build per platform. Durations are computed from transitions, never typed in. Published weekly statistics are reproducible. Events can arrive late or twice. A developer sees only their own apps; reviewer identities are never exposed in developer views or in published statistics.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, shares and platform lists are hypothetical. State names are this exercise's. Message contents are out of scope for analytics. The review tools themselves are not part of the design.
sections.criteria: Version, build, submission and review episode modelled separately; an append-only, deduplicated state history; durations defined as pairs of events with clear clock-stops; rates with explicit denominators and cohorts; guideline citations as a many-to-many table with counting rules; resubmission links; percentiles over skewed durations with a stated finality; developer-scoped views without reviewer identity; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Does "time in review" include time in the queue?
clarifications.a: No. Define waiting and in-review time separately; developers mostly care about the total.

clarifications.q: Is a metadata-only rejection a new submission when fixed?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, the fix continues the same submission with a new review episode. State how your rates treat it.

clarifications.q: Is a submission the developer removed before review a rejection?
clarifications.a: No. It is its own outcome. Decide whether it is in any denominator.

clarifications.q: Can one rejection cite several guidelines?
clarifications.a: Yes, often two or three.

clarifications.q: Which week does a submission belong to in the published statistic?
clarifications.a: Your choice: the week it entered the queue or the week it was decided. State it and why.

hints: Separate the version (what is being shipped), the build (the binary), the submission (a request to review) and the review episode (one pass through review). Durations come from the transitions.
Write each duration as a pair of events, and state what stops the clock (waiting on the developer is not review time).
Every rate needs a stated denominator and cohort; first pass means the first episode of a version, not of a submission.
followups: Walk one version: build 41 submitted, rejected citing two guidelines, developer replies, build 42 uploaded and submitted, rejected for metadata only, metadata fixed, approved, held for developer release, released. List the rows and every duration.
Define the weekly "most submissions are reviewed within N hours" statistic: which percentile, which durations, which cohort, and when is a week final?
First-pass approval rate: what is the denominator when developers remove submissions before review, and when a version is approved only after a metadata fix?
At {{submissions_per_week}} submissions a week, how do you serve each developer's history and the platform-wide percentiles, and what is precomputed?
Expedited reviews (about {{expedite_share}}) jump the queue. How do you keep them from flattering the published waiting-time statistic, or should they?

rules.ask: A submission was rejected, fixed and approved. With one status column, how do you compute how long it waited before each decision?
