Review times are skewed. What does one submission stuck for nine days do to your weekly average, and what would you publish instead?
What exactly is the denominator: submissions, review episodes or versions? Where do developer-removed submissions go?
One rejection cites three guidelines. Is that one rejection or three in "rejections by guideline", and what does the total across guidelines mean?
How is a resubmission linked to the rejected one when the developer uploads a new build, and when they only fix metadata?

incidents: The published median time in review doubled overnight: an upstream release renamed a state, and the duration job started counting waiting time as review time for {{platforms}} submissions alike.

The first-pass rejection rate, usually about {{rejection_share}}, fell sharply overnight and the team celebrated: metadata-only fixes had started arriving as new submissions, and each approved fix was counted as the first pass of a version.
In a holiday week, expedited reviews (normally about {{expedite_share}}) multiplied. The published waiting time improved while ordinary submissions waited longer than ever.

templates.title: Phased release adoption — devices on the new build, day by day
templates.subtopic: date spine, state from an action log, running counts that skip paused days, device-day grain

sections.scenario: A developer ships an update to {{app_count}} through an app store's phased release. This exercise's rule, modelled on public developer documentation (check current docs): an update reaches devices with automatic updates on over seven phase days, at the percentages in phase_schedule (phase day 1 is 1%, phase day 7 is 100%); the developer can pause and resume, and can release to everyone at any time; anyone can still update by hand from the store, so adoption can run ahead of the schedule. The developer's analytics team wants, for every day of each release, how much of the active device base is really running the new code. The model: apps, app_builds (every build with its version string and an increasing build_number), phase_schedule, phased_release_log (one row per action: start, pause, resume, release_all, at most one per app per date) and app_sessions (one row per session, with the version it ran). {{day_rule}}
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns app_id, activity_date, phase_day, release_state, release_pct, active_devices, devices_on_new, share_on_new: one row per app and date, from the date of the app's start action through the date its phased release ends, but never after {{report_end}}, ordered by app_id, activity_date. A date's release_state comes from the latest log action on or before it: start or resume → active, pause → paused, release_all → complete. phase_day is the number of active dates from the start date through this date (a paused date does not advance it). release_pct is the phase_schedule percentage for phase_day, or 100 when the state is complete. The phased release ends on the first date whose phase_day is 7 or whose state is complete; that date is the last row. active_devices is the number of distinct devices with a session for the app on that date, and devices_on_new how many of them had at least one session that date on the build in the log (the phased build) or a later build of the same app (a higher build_number). share_on_new is 100 × devices_on_new / active_devices rounded to 2 decimal places, or NULL when no device was active; such a date still appears, with 0 and 0.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Each app has exactly one phased release in the log. Every session's app_version is listed in app_builds. The sample has {{sessions}} sessions; a production version of this report reads billions of session rows a day.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical apps, versions, builds, devices and sessions; the seven-day schedule is this exercise's. device_id is a pseudonymous identifier from the developer's own analytics, meaningful only within this data set. Devices never go back to an older build.
sections.criteria: A date spine from the log so empty and paused dates appear; state from the latest action on or before each date; phase_day as a running count of active dates only; the end date from the first day 7 or release_all, capped by the report end; sessions reduced to the device-day grain with "any session on the phased build or later" by build_number; at the hardest level, dates in each app's report time zone and no text comparison of versions; numeric division with NULL for no devices; deterministic ordering; can discuss crash comparisons, manual updates and late data.

clarifications.q: A device ran the old version in the morning and the new one after updating at noon. Is it on the new build that day?
clarifications.a: Yes. At least one session on the phased build or later is enough.

clarifications.q: Does a paused date appear?
clarifications.a: Yes, with state paused, and the same phase_day and release_pct as the active date before it.

clarifications.q: What is phase_day on the release_all date?
clarifications.a: The number of active dates before it; that date is not active. Its release_pct is 100 and it is the last row.

clarifications.q: Should dates with no sessions at all appear?
clarifications.a: Yes, with active_devices 0, devices_on_new 0 and a NULL share. A missing date looks like a gap in the rollout chart.

clarifications.q: Do sessions before the start date matter?
clarifications.a: No row comes before the start date. They are in the table only because devices were active then.

hints: Build the dates first: generate_series from each app's start date to the report end. Attach the latest log action on or before each date (a LATERAL subquery with ORDER BY … LIMIT 1 works), then a running COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …) gives phase_day.
Reduce sessions to one row per app, date and device with BOOL_OR(…) before counting anything; then LEFT JOIN that to the dates.
The end date depends on the running count, so compute it in a window over the finished calendar (MIN(date) FILTER (…) OVER (PARTITION BY app_id)) and filter after it.
followups: The developer paused because crash reports rose on the new build. What would you add to this query to compare crash-free sessions on the new and old builds per day, and why is a 1% phased cohort plus manual updaters not a random sample?
How much of share_on_new is the phased release and how much is people updating by hand? What can and can't this data tell you?
At billions of sessions a day, what daily rollup would you keep so this report runs in seconds, and what does a session that arrives two days late do to a day already published?
From this output, define "days to 90% adoption" per release so that releases with and without pauses can be compared fairly.

rules.ask: After your LEFT JOIN to the dates, what does COUNT(*) return for a date with no sessions, and does it count devices or sessions?
If phase_day comes from numbering the dates since the start, what does a paused date do to it, and to the date the release ends?
As text, how do '…9.6' and '…10.0' compare, and what happens when a hotfix build ships after the phased build?
Which dates disappear when the calendar is inner-joined to sessions, and why are those the dates a rollout chart most needs?
For an app that reports in Asia/Kolkata, which date does a session at 20:00 UTC belong to, and in which zone are the log's dates?

incidents: After a pause for a crash spike, a dashboard that numbered days since the start showed the release at 50% when the schedule had reached 5%. The go/no-go call for the next phase was made on that number.

An analytics SDK update began sending versions with a build suffix for some sessions. Those sessions matched no row in app_builds, an inner join dropped them, and the share on the new build fell on the day a fix was being judged.

templates.title: Local differential privacy telemetry with per-day contribution limits
templates.subtopic: local differential privacy, privacy budgets, release rules

sections.scenario: A device maker wants to learn which of {{domain_size}} possible values are most common across its devices each day (for example, which built-in features or settings were used) without learning any one device's value. About {{devices}} devices whose owners opted in to sharing usage statistics take part. The technique chosen is local differential privacy: each device randomises its own answer before it leaves the device, so any single report is deniable, and the server can only estimate population totals. In this exercise each report is randomised with a privacy parameter ε = {{epsilon}}, and a device may send at most {{reports_per_day}} reports per day across all use cases.
sections.problem: Design the system end to end: what runs on the device (choosing what to report, randomising it, enforcing the per-day limit, queuing and uploading), the ingestion path, how the server turns noisy reports into estimates, and the rules for what may be released to product teams and in what form. Say how a new use case is approved and given part of the daily limit, and how you would show, after the fact, that no device exceeded it.
sections.constraints: No report may carry a device identifier, account identifier or anything that links two reports from the same device. The per-day limit must hold even if the device is offline for a week, its clock is changed, or an upload is retried. Daily estimates are published by 09:00 UTC for the previous UTC day. Raw reports are kept for at most 30 days; estimates may be kept longer.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, parameters and the use case are hypothetical, and the design describes a general technique, not how any company implements it. Devices are online at least once a day on most days. A report is a few hundred bytes.
sections.criteria: On-device randomisation with a named mechanism, an explicit debiasing estimator and its error; a large-domain strategy (hashing into a sketch); the per-day limit enforced on the device with a persisted ledger that survives clock changes and offline periods, and randomised values stored and resent rather than regenerated; ingestion that strips network and transport metadata and keeps no linkable identifier; release rules (minimum population, error-based thresholds, confidence intervals, coarse slices only) and a governance process for new use cases sharing the budget; ways to verify the limit held; adapts to each incident with containment, purge and prevention.

clarifications.q: Which randomisation mechanism must I use?
clarifications.a: Your choice; say how its estimate is debiased and how its error grows with the size of the value domain.

clarifications.q: Can the server know which country or device model a report came from?
clarifications.a: Only if the device includes it, and every attribute you add makes reports easier to link. Decide and justify.

clarifications.q: Is the limit per use case or per device?
clarifications.a: Per device per day, across every use case. Use cases share it.

clarifications.q: Who consumes the estimates?
clarifications.a: Product teams, through dashboards and tables. They will ask for finer slices than you want to give.

clarifications.q: Can a device skip a day?
clarifications.a: Yes. Skipping is always allowed; exceeding the limit never is.

hints: Write down the estimator first: given n reports and your mechanism's probabilities, how do you turn an observed count into an unbiased estimate, and what is its standard error?
The device is the only place the limit can be enforced, because the server cannot link reports. Think about what the device must remember and what it must never regenerate.
A large value domain makes plain randomised response useless; consider hashing into a sketch so the error depends on the sketch width rather than on {{domain_size}}.
followups: Walk through one report from the moment the value is chosen to the moment it contributes to a published estimate. What is stored where, and for how long?
What is the smallest true count your system can distinguish from zero at your chosen ε and n, and how does that shape what you release?
An upload fails three times. What does the device send on the fourth attempt, and why does that matter for privacy?
A product team wants yesterday's top values per device model and per locale. What do you give them, and what do you refuse?
How do you discover frequently used values that are not in the dictionary of {{domain_size}} known values, without breaking the daily limit?

rules.ask: Which field lets you deduplicate retries, and what stops that same field from linking two reports from one device?
With {{domain_size}} possible values, what is the probability a device reports its true value at ε = {{epsilon}}, and what does that do to your estimate's error?
Two popular values collide in the same hash cells. How does that show up in the estimates, and how do you reduce it?
How do you choose the threshold from n and ε, and what do you show a product team for a value below it?
Does a retried upload carry the same randomised value or a new one? Show me what an observer could learn from each choice.

incidents: A client release regenerates a fresh randomised report on every upload retry instead of resending the stored one. On flaky networks some devices send the same day's value five times with independent noise, which is far beyond {{reports_per_day}} reports per day.

A product team's dashboard slices yesterday's estimates by device model and locale. One combination has about 3,000 reporting devices; the published table shows negative counts and a "top value" that is not plausible.
The load balancer in front of the ingestion endpoint, run by another team, has been writing the source network address of every report to its access logs for six weeks.

templates.title: Royalty-ready play counts with late offline plays and restatements
templates.subtopic: qualifying plays, late data, monthly statements, bitemporal restatement

sections.scenario: A music streaming service records about {{plays_per_day}} plays a day across {{territories}} territories. Rights holders are paid from monthly usage statements: for each territory and recording, the number of qualifying plays in the calendar month. In this exercise's rules a play qualifies when at least {{qualify_seconds}} seconds of it were heard, the listener's subscription was valid at the time, and the play is attributed to the territory of the listener's account storefront at the time of the play. Listeners download music and play it offline; offline plays are logged on the device and accepted if they reach the service within {{offline_days}} days. Statements for a month are due {{close_days}} days after it ends.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline from the play event on a device to the monthly statements: event capture and upload, deduplication, the qualifying-play rule, territory attribution, the monthly aggregation per territory and recording, and what happens to plays that arrive, or are found to be invalid, after a statement has been sent. Be precise about what a statement is (a frozen, versioned artefact) and how later changes reach rights holders.
sections.constraints: A statement, once sent, is never edited; later changes appear as adjustment lines on a later statement that name the period they correct. Every number on a statement must be traceable to the plays behind it. Devices retry uploads, so the same play can arrive several times. A listener's storefront can change mid-month.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, rules and deadlines are hypothetical and belong to this exercise; check current docs for any real service's rules. Each recording has a stable identifier and the catalogue maps it to rights holders per territory. The device clock is usually right but not always.
sections.criteria: Device-generated play ids with idempotent ingestion; event time and arrival time on every play, with clock validation; qualifying rules applied with the subscription and storefront that were valid at play time (effective-dated dimensions); statements as frozen, versioned, as-of queries; adjustments computed as differences between current knowledge and what was reported, never edits; traceability from statement line to plays; partitioning and incremental aggregation that scale with volume; a reconciliation process with rights holders by reason; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, correction through adjustments and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does a seek or pause end a play?
clarifications.a: In this exercise a play is one playback of one track; seeks and pauses inside it do not start a new play. Repeating the track does.

clarifications.q: Which date does a play belong to?
clarifications.a: The month of the play in UTC, by the time the device says it started, validated against when it reached you.

clarifications.q: What if the subscription lapsed while the device was offline?
clarifications.a: Plays after the lapse do not qualify, even if they arrive later.

clarifications.q: Do rights holders see individual plays?
clarifications.a: No. They see counts per territory and recording; they can ask for an audit of how a number was produced.

clarifications.q: Can a play be removed after it was reported?
clarifications.a: Yes, for example when listening is later found to be automated. That is an adjustment.

hints: Keep two times on every play: when it happened and when you learned of it. A statement is a query "as known at" its close time.
Give each play an identifier made on the device when playback starts; retries reuse it.
Adjustments are a difference between what is known now about a past month and what was reported for it. Compute them, do not type them.
followups: Walk through one offline play that reaches you 20 days after month end. Where does it land, and how does it appear to the rights holder?
How do you prove that a statement's total for one recording and territory equals the qualifying plays behind it, months later?
A listener changes storefront on the 14th. Which territory gets their plays, and what data do you need to decide?
Fraud review removes three months of plays from a set of accounts. Walk through the adjustment lines that result.
Monthly volume is growing 40% a year. Which part of your pipeline stops scaling first, and what do you change?

rules.ask: A statement for last month was built from the rows you just overwrote. How do you reproduce exactly what was sent?
A device's clock is two months behind. Its plays arrive today stamped in an old month. What do you do with them?
Statements are monthly. What does streaming buy you here, and what still has to be batch?
An app version sends each offline play twice on reconnect with two different play ids. Does your deduplication catch it? How would you find out?
How long do you keep each frozen statement's inputs, and what does that cost at {{plays_per_day}} plays a day?

incidents: An app version sends each offline play twice when it reconnects, once from its play log and once from a retry path, with two different play ids. It has been live for three weeks, across a month boundary, and last month's statements are already out.
Two days before statements are due ({{close_days}} days after month end), a rights holder's own figures show 12% more plays than yours for one album in one territory.
Fraud review flags 40,000 accounts whose plays over the last three months came from automated listening. All three months have been reported.

templates.title: Service analytics for end-to-end encrypted sync
templates.subtopic: end-to-end encryption, metadata minimisation, client-side telemetry

sections.scenario: A cloud sync service keeps users' {{data_kind}} in step across their devices: {{accounts}} accounts with about {{devices_per_account}} devices each. For accounts that turn on end-to-end encryption, records are encrypted on the device with keys the service never holds; the server stores and forwards ciphertext. The service team still has to run the service: know whether sync is fast and reliable, plan storage, find the client release that broke something, and answer product questions. Service logs are kept for {{log_days}} days.
sections.problem: Design the analytics and observability for this service. Say what the server can observe without the keys (and what it should not keep even though it can), what clients may report about themselves and under what consent, how the metrics the team needs are computed (sync latency, conflict and failure rates, storage growth, active devices), how a broken client release is detected when the server cannot read what it stored, and which product questions the design refuses to answer, with what you offer instead.
sections.constraints: No content, record names, file names or anything derived from them may reach the server in readable form. Metadata the server must have (record sizes, timestamps, device and account identifiers) is minimised and kept no longer than needed. Client telemetry is opt-in and contains no content. Support staff must never be able to see a user's data.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, retention periods and the data kind are hypothetical; the design describes general techniques, not how any company builds its service. Clients run a recent release within about two weeks of it shipping.
sections.criteria: A clear inventory of server-observable metadata with a minimisation plan (allowlisted log fields, coarsened timestamps, padding where exact sizes would reveal content, short retention); service metrics computed from request metadata; opt-in client telemetry with fixed, content-free schemas for decrypt failures, conflicts and latency per client version; staged client rollout and recoverable ciphertext versions; refusal of content questions or on-device aggregation under a privacy mechanism with thresholds; awareness that convergent encryption and metadata reveal information; support flows that never expose data; adapts to each incident with containment, purge and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does the server see record sizes?
clarifications.a: It stores ciphertext, so it knows its length unless you pad. Decide whether that matters.

clarifications.q: Can clients send crash and error reports?
clarifications.a: Only from users who opted in to sharing diagnostics, and only with the fields you specify.

clarifications.q: Do we keep old versions of records?
clarifications.a: For a short time, as ciphertext, so a bad write can be rolled back by the user's own devices.

clarifications.q: Can the server deduplicate identical attachments across users?
clarifications.a: Only if it can tell they are identical. Think about what that reveals.

hints: List what the server sees on every request (who, when, how big, which device, which client version, the outcome) and separate what you need from what you merely could keep.
The only component that knows whether a record decrypted correctly is another client. Failure signals have to come from there.
For a product question about content, the answer is either "we do not ask it" or "the device computes an aggregate and reports it under a privacy mechanism".
followups: Define "sync latency" precisely using only what the server and an opted-in client can observe.
A client release writes records that other devices cannot decrypt. How do you find out within an hour, and how do users get their data back?
Which metadata would you pad, coarsen or drop, and what does each choice cost in storage or debuggability?
Product wants to know how many users use a new formatting feature inside their {{data_kind}}. What do you build, or what do you say?
A regulator asks what the service knows about one account. What can you list, and from where?

rules.ask: Which fields of a sync request end up in your logs, and what stops a client from putting a record name in one of them?
Only opted-in clients report. How do you know the opted-in population is representative of the release you are judging?
If identical attachments produce identical ciphertext, what can the server learn about two accounts?
A user says half their {{data_kind}} vanished from one device. What can support see, and what do they ask the user to do?
Which question would you answer that way, with what minimum population, and who decides the parameters?

incidents: A client release starts uploading records that the user's other devices cannot decrypt. The server sees ordinary writes and a normal error rate; support tickets say {{data_kind}} are "missing" on second devices.
A debug field added to sync requests has carried record names in plain text for five days, and the service has been writing it to logs kept for {{log_days}} days.
Storage grows 30% faster than forecast for a month. Nobody can read the content, so nobody can say what is growing.

templates.title: Equalised storefront pricing and what a customer paid when
templates.subtopic: currencies, taxes, scheduled changes, auditability

sections.scenario: An app marketplace sells {{products}} paid apps, in-app purchases and subscriptions in {{storefronts}} storefronts and {{currencies}} currencies. In this exercise's rules (check current docs for any real store), a developer picks a price point in one base storefront and the system generates equalised prices for every other storefront from exchange rates and local taxes; the developer may override any storefront, schedule a price change to start on a future date, and, for subscriptions, existing subscribers keep their price until a change is applied to them. Exchange rates and tax rates change, and equalised prices are regenerated when they do. Purchases peak at {{purchases_per_second}} per second.
sections.problem: Design the pricing system: the model for price points, base prices, generated and overridden prices, and schedules; how regenerated prices flow out when rates or taxes change; the read path that gives a product page and checkout the price in force; and the record that answers, years later, exactly what a customer paid, in which currency, with which tax, and why that was the price.
sections.constraints: The product page and checkout must agree: a customer is never charged a price other than the one shown. Checkout price lookup p99 under 30 ms. A scheduled change takes effect at a precise instant that you must define. Developers' proceeds reports must be reproducible for any past period. Price history is kept for at least seven years.
sections.assumptions: All counts, rates, rules and latency targets are hypothetical and belong to this exercise. Exchange rates come from an outside provider once a day. Tax rules per storefront are maintained by a separate team that publishes changes with an effective date.
sections.criteria: A bitemporal, effective-dated model for base prices, generated prices, overrides and schedules; money in minor units with per-currency exponents; a defined effective instant per storefront that developers and customers can understand; regeneration as a staged, reviewed batch with guardrails on the size of change and a publish switch; a fast read path (precomputed price per product and storefront, versioned) with price quotes so the page and checkout agree; immutable purchase records that carry price, currency, tax, price row version and quote id; reproducible proceeds; adapts to each incident with containment, a customer-fair remedy and prevention.

clarifications.q: When does a scheduled change start: UTC midnight or each storefront's local midnight?
clarifications.a: You decide and say how a developer and a customer would understand it.

clarifications.q: Do currencies all have two decimal places?
clarifications.a: No. Some have none, a few have three.

clarifications.q: Are prices shown tax-inclusive?
clarifications.a: In most storefronts in this exercise, yes; in a few, tax is added at checkout.

clarifications.q: Can a customer see one price on the page and pay another?
clarifications.a: Only if the price changed between the two; say what you do in that window.

clarifications.q: How often do rates move enough to matter?
clarifications.a: Usually a few storefronts a month; occasionally a currency moves sharply in a day.

hints: Model prices as effective-dated rows with both a valid-from instant and the time the row was recorded; "the price on a date" and "what we believed on a date" are different questions.
Store money in minor units with the currency's own exponent, and test the zero-decimal currencies.
Give the checkout a price quote with an identifier and an expiry, and charge the quote, not a fresh lookup.
followups: A developer schedules a price increase for the first of next month. Walk through what is stored, when each storefront switches, and what a customer mid-checkout at that instant pays.
An exchange-rate update would move prices in 40 storefronts. What checks run before any new price goes live?
How do you answer "what did this customer pay for this subscription in March three years ago, and why that price"?
A tax rate rises in one storefront from a date next week. What changes: prices, proceeds, or both, and who chooses?
How do you serve checkout lookups at {{purchases_per_second}} purchases per second while price regeneration rewrites millions of rows?

rules.ask: Show me how a price in a zero-decimal currency is stored and converted, and where a factor of 100 could slip in.
A scheduled change goes live at midnight while product pages still serve the cached old price. What does a customer who buys at 00:01 pay?
For a storefront eight hours ahead of UTC, at what local time does your change take effect, and is that what the developer expected?
An auditor asks for the price in force last June in one storefront. Where does that answer come from once rows have been updated?
How long is the quote valid, and what happens when a scheduled change lands inside it?

incidents: A scheduled price increase for a popular subscription takes effect at 00:00 UTC on the first of the month. In storefronts ahead of UTC the old price stayed on sale until the morning of the 1st local time, and the developer asks why; in storefronts behind UTC customers were charged the new price on what was still their 31st, and they complain.
A regeneration after an exchange-rate update produced prices one hundred times too low in one zero-decimal currency. Purchases ran at the wrong price for three hours before anyone noticed.

One storefront announces a tax rate change effective in nine days. Prices for {{products}} products there must be regenerated or developers' proceeds will fall, and last quarter's reports must still show the old rate.

templates.title: Daily health totals from overlapping watch and phone samples, shared only with consent
templates.subtopic: interval merging across sources, local-day totals, consent-scoped sharing

sections.scenario: A health data feature collects {{metric}} and other measures for {{users}} users from about {{sources}} sources each: a watch, a phone, and connected apps or devices the user allowed to write data. In this exercise each source writes samples of the form (start, end, value, unit, source), and sources overlap: a user carrying a phone while wearing a watch has two sources measuring the same minutes. Users see daily totals per measure. They can share any of {{share_types}} data types with a family member or an app, and stop sharing at any time.
sections.problem: Design how samples are stored and synced across a user's devices, how overlapping samples from several sources become one daily total without double counting, how a "day" is defined for a user who travels, and how sharing works: what a grant contains, what a recipient can read, what happens to history and to copies when a grant is revoked. Say where each computation runs (on the device or on a server) and why.
sections.constraints: Health data is among the most sensitive data a person has: it is never used for any purpose the user has not turned on, and it is encrypted in transit and at rest. A total shown on two of the user's devices must agree after they sync. A user can delete any sample or source, and deleted data must disappear from totals and from what recipients see. Samples can arrive days late from a device that was off.
sections.assumptions: All volumes and counts are hypothetical. This exercise's merge rule: the user orders their sources by priority, and for any interval the highest-priority source that has data for it is used. Nothing here describes what any real device measures or how any company's health features work.
sections.criteria: Samples as the encrypted source of truth with sync and late arrival; an interval-sweep merge by user-ordered source priority with even-spread proration and recomputation of affected days; local days from the offset stored with each sample, splitting samples that cross midnight; a reasoned choice of on-device versus server computation that minimises who can read values; grants with explicit scope, history visibility and revocation, enforced at read and at sync, with honest limits on recipient copies; deletion that propagates to totals and recipients; new sources added at the lowest priority by default; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, correction and prevention.

clarifications.q: A watch sample covers 10:00–10:10 and a phone sample 10:05–10:20. How do I split them?
clarifications.a: Assume a sample's value is spread evenly over its interval, and say what that assumption costs.

clarifications.q: Which time zone defines a day?
clarifications.a: The user's local time where the sample was recorded; you need to keep that offset with the sample.

clarifications.q: Does a recipient see raw samples or daily totals?
clarifications.a: The grant says, per data type.

clarifications.q: When access is revoked, must the recipient's existing copy disappear?
clarifications.a: Say what you can guarantee and what you cannot, and how you would tell the user.

clarifications.q: Can a new source be added mid-day?
clarifications.a: Yes, and it may write samples for the past.

hints: Merging by priority is an interval sweep: cut the day into pieces at every sample boundary and take, for each piece, the highest-priority source that covers it.
Totals are derived data. Store samples as the truth and make totals recomputable for any day touched by a late sample, an edit or a priority change.
A grant is a row with a recipient, data types, a start of visibility and a revocation time; enforce it where data is read, and think about keys if the server cannot read the data.
followups: Walk through merging one hour with a watch, a phone and a connected app all reporting {{metric}}, including a partial overlap.
A user flies across eight time zones. Which day does each sample belong to, and what does the user see for the travel days?
The user reorders source priority. What is recomputed, where, and how fast do totals on all devices agree?
Where would you compute totals: on each device, on a server, or both? What does each choice mean for privacy and consistency?
A user grants a family member access to {{metric}} from today, then revokes it a month later. What can the family member still see, and what did you promise the user?

rules.ask: The watch and phone both reported 10:00 to 10:30. What does a plain sum show, and what should it show?
A sample runs from 23:50 to 00:20 local time on a day the user crossed a time zone. Which day gets which part?
Which of your server components can read health values, and why does that one need to?
The recipient's device was offline when access was revoked. What happens when it comes back online?
A connected app copies the watch's own samples into the store under its own name. How does your merge treat those copies?

incidents: A newly connected app writes {{metric}} samples copied from the watch's data under its own source name. For two days, totals for its users are about double.
Users who flew across eight time zones see two days with odd totals: one about 30% too high, the next nearly empty.
A user stops sharing {{metric}} with a family member; three days later the family member's phone, which had been offline, still shows the user's last week of data.

templates.title: Getting help from other teams for an unannounced project you cannot explain
templates.subtopic: secrecy, honesty, cross-team requests

ask: a new field in a shared device-event schema
three times the usual capacity on a shared ingestion pipeline
keeping an old data export running six months past its retirement date

sections.scenario: You lead the data work for a product that has not been announced. A small, named group of people knows about it; everyone else must not. To be ready for launch you need {{ask}}, which depends on {{teams}} teams outside that group, within {{weeks}} weeks. Their roadmaps are full, and their first question is always "what is it for?". You may not tell them.
sections.problem: How would you get what you need? Cover what you can say and what you cannot, how you frame the request so it can be judged on its merits, how you answer questions without misleading anyone, who you bring in and through what process, what you do if a team says no, and how you leave the relationship when the product is announced. Then describe a real situation where you needed something from people you could not give full context to, or any request you had to make with limited information, with its outcome; or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You may not disclose the project, and you may not add anyone to the group that knows about it yourself; there is a process for that, run by the project's sponsor. You must not give a false reason. Your own team could build part of a workaround, but the systems involved belong to the other teams.
sections.assumptions: The situation, timings and team counts are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Separates what is needed (precise, costed, dated) from why, and shares everything except the why; never invents a reason; uses the sponsor's process to bring in the minimum set of people, with a crisp ask; offers something real in return (engineering help, a clear cost estimate, flexibility on dates); a sound decision on workarounds that weighs ownership and launch risk; repairs and acknowledges the relationship after the announcement; real example with honest handling of limited information, personal contribution and an outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Can I tell the other teams' managers?
clarifications.a: Only if they are added to the group through the sponsor's process. You can ask for that.

clarifications.q: Is there a sponsor who knows?
clarifications.a: A director, with very little spare time.

clarifications.q: Can I say it is for something else?
clarifications.a: You decide what you say; everything you say will be remembered after the launch.

clarifications.q: Have these teams helped you before?
clarifications.a: Two of them have; one has not worked with your team at all.

hints: Separate the request from the reason: what exactly you need, by when, at what cost to them, and what happens if it is late. Most of that can be shared.
"I cannot say why, and I will not pretend otherwise" is a statement you can make honestly. A made-up reason cannot be taken back.
Find the smallest number of people who must know, and ask the sponsor to bring exactly those in.
followups: Write the first message you would send to the team that has never worked with you.
One team says they will only prioritise it if they know what it is for. What do you do?
The sponsor will not add anyone to the group. Do you build a workaround on another team's system? What does it cost later?
After the announcement, a team lead tells you they felt used. What do you say, and what would you have done differently?
In your real example, what did you decide not to say, and how did that affect the outcome?

rules.ask: The product is announced and they learn the real reason. What do they now believe about everything else you tell them?
What exactly do you ask the sponsor to decide, and what do you bring them so it takes ten minutes, not an hour?
That system belongs to another team. Who is on call for your workaround at launch, and who removes it afterwards?
What did you give the other team in return, and how would they describe the exchange?
Which part of that did you personally do or decide?

templates.title: A fixed hardware launch date and a data pipeline that is not ready
templates.subtopic: day-one requirements, risk, recoverability

gap: the activation-metrics pipeline has been tested at only half the expected launch-day volume
the new model's diagnostic events have no schema validation and no backfill path
launch-day dashboards depend on a device-to-account join that has never run at full scale

sections.scenario: A new device launches on a date that will not move. Your team owns the pipeline that turns launch-day events (activations, setup completions, early diagnostics) into the numbers {{stakeholder}} will use in the first week. With {{weeks_left}} weeks to go, {{gap}}. Your team also has a list of smaller features stakeholders were promised for day one.
sections.problem: How do you decide what ships on day one and what does not? Cover how you find out what is truly required on launch day versus in the first week or month, what must be right from the first event because it cannot be reconstructed later, how you reduce the risk of the gap in the time left, what you cut and how you tell the people who were promised it, what you prepare for launch day itself, and how you report status honestly as the date approaches. Then describe a real fixed-date delivery you led where scope had to give, with the outcome, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The launch date cannot move. You cannot hire for this. Data lost on launch day (events never captured) cannot be recovered; derived numbers can be recomputed if the raw events exist.
sections.assumptions: The situation and timings are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Classifies work by recoverability, protecting raw capture first and treating derived numbers as recomputable; makes the gap a measured risk (load tests with synthetic events, a defined fallback) and reduces it with the time left; cuts scope early and openly with the people who were promised it, through the right decision-maker; prepares launch day (runbooks, on-call, degraded modes, who decides); reports status against stated thresholds rather than optimism; protects the team from unsustainable pushes; real example with scope trade-offs, personal decisions and an outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Who decided which features were promised?
clarifications.a: Your predecessor, with each stakeholder separately. Nobody has seen the whole list at once.

clarifications.q: Can launch-day numbers arrive late?
clarifications.a: Some can; {{stakeholder}} say all of them are urgent.

clarifications.q: Can you run a test at launch volume?
clarifications.a: With synthetic events, if you build the generator.

clarifications.q: Who can approve cutting a promised feature?
clarifications.a: The stakeholder who asked for it, or the launch's overall lead.

hints: Sort everything by "cannot be recovered if wrong on day one" versus "can be recomputed or added later". Raw capture is in the first group; most dashboards are in the second.
Turn the gap into a measured risk: what fails, at what volume, and what the fallback is.
A list cut once, early and in the open, costs less trust than features that quietly slip on launch day.
followups: Walk me through the list: what is in the day-one group and why?
How do you reduce the risk of the gap in {{weeks_left}} weeks, and what is the fallback if it still fails on the day?
A stakeholder refuses to accept a cut. What do you do?
Two days before launch your load test fails at 80% of expected volume. Who do you tell, what do you change, and what do you not change?
In your real example, what did you cut, who did you tell and how, and how did it turn out?

rules.ask: The team works weekends for {{weeks_left}} weeks. What breaks on launch day because people are exhausted, and is that a plan?
Who agreed to that cut, and what did you give them instead?
If capture is right but processing fails on launch day, how long until the numbers exist, and who knows that in advance?
What would have made you report red, and when did you decide that threshold?
Which call did you personally make, and what did it cost?

templates.title: Two strong engineers in a long-running conflict over ownership
templates.subtopic: conflict, ownership boundaries, decision rights

area: the on-call rotation for the sync analytics pipeline
effect: design reviews that stall for weeks
two half-built versions of the same component
a new engineer who has asked to move to another team

sections.scenario: You lead a data engineering team of eight. Two of its strongest engineers have disagreed for {{months}} months about who owns {{area}} and how it should change. Both are right about some things. Each has started making decisions about it without the other. The result so far is {{effect}}. Neither has asked you to intervene; both have complained about the other to you, separately.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you find out what the disagreement is actually about, how you talk to each of them and when together, how ownership and decision rights for {{area}} are settled and written down, how you deal with the damage already done, what you do if one of them will not accept the outcome, and how you would know it is resolved. Then describe a real conflict between people you led or worked closely with, what you did and how it ended, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You cannot afford to lose either engineer. You cannot move either of them to another team. Delivery commitments on {{area}} continue.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Diagnoses before acting (separate conversations, understanding each position, separating direction from ownership from behaviour); owns the leader's part in leaving ownership undefined; settles ownership and decision rights explicitly, in writing, with a disagreement path; treats both engineers fairly and keeps them both; addresses the damage (stalled reviews, duplicated work, the team taking sides) concretely; handles continued relitigation directly and early; real example with personal actions, an outcome and an honest lesson, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Do they disagree on technical direction or on who decides?
clarifications.a: Both, and they mix them up.

clarifications.q: Have you ever said who owns {{area}}?
clarifications.a: No. It was shared by default.

clarifications.q: Is anyone else affected?
clarifications.a: Yes, as described; others have started taking sides.

clarifications.q: Is either behaving unprofessionally?
clarifications.a: Not openly. They are curt in reviews and avoid each other.

hints: Separate three questions: what the right technical direction is, who decides it, and how the two of them work together. They need different answers.
Unclear ownership is usually the leader's gap, not the engineers'. Say so.
Make the decision rule explicit and written, with a way to disagree and still commit.
followups: What do you say in the first one-to-one with each of them?
How do you decide who owns {{area}}, or do you split it? What makes a split work?
One of them disagrees with the outcome and keeps relitigating it in reviews. What do you do?
How do you repair the effect on the rest of the team, including {{effect}}?
In your real example, what did you get wrong, and what would you do differently?

rules.ask: What do you need to know from each of them before you put them in a room, and what is the outcome you want from that meeting?
Where exactly is the boundary, and who decides when a change crosses it?
What has either of them done that is a performance problem rather than a disagreement? What evidence do you have?
Which part of this is yours to fix, and what would you ask your manager for?
What did you personally say or decide, and how did each of them react?

templates.title: A team you depend on deprioritises the interface your launch needs
templates.subtopic: negotiation, contingency planning, escalation

interface: a daily export of subscription state changes
a streaming feed of app review outcomes
a batch interface for storefront price schedules
reason: a security fix that is taking their whole team
a reorganisation that moved two of their engineers elsewhere
a launch of their own on the same date

sections.scenario: Your team is building reporting for a developer-facing launch {{weeks}} weeks away. It depends on {{interface}} from another team, which agreed last quarter to build it. This week they told you it is deprioritised because of {{reason}}. Their reason is legitimate. Your launch date has been announced to developers.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you establish what is now realistic from their side, what options exist (a smaller interface, your team doing part of the work, a temporary alternative source, moving part of your launch), how you negotiate without damaging the relationship, when and how you escalate, how you tell the developers or your stakeholders if something changes, and how you avoid this kind of dependency risk next time. Then describe a real case where a dependency fell through and what you did, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You have no authority over the other team. Your own team has three engineers available. Any temporary alternative source must be removed after the real interface exists.
sections.assumptions: The situation and timings are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Accepts the other team's reason and works from what is now feasible; defines a minimal interface; prices options (minimal version, contributing engineers with review and ownership agreed, a temporary source with known limits and a removal plan, partial launch); negotiates with something to offer; escalates with two clear options and a recommendation, together with the other lead where possible; honest communication of changes to stakeholders or developers; prevention through dependency agreements with checkpoints; real example with personal contribution and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is there a written agreement?
clarifications.a: A line in last quarter's plan and a design document both teams signed off.

clarifications.q: Could your engineers work in their codebase?
clarifications.a: Possibly, if they accept and review the changes.

clarifications.q: Is there another source for the same data?
clarifications.a: A nightly report built for a different purpose, close but not identical.

clarifications.q: Who sets priorities for both teams?
clarifications.a: A shared director two levels up.

hints: Start from what they can still do, not from what they promised. Ask for the smallest version that unblocks you.
Price every option in engineer-weeks, risk and what it leaves behind after launch.
Escalation asks a person with authority to choose between two clearly stated options; it is not a complaint.
followups: What do you ask for in your first conversation with the other team's lead?
You propose that your engineers build the interface in their codebase. They are worried about reviewing it and owning it afterwards. How do you address that?
The nightly report is close but not identical. Do you launch on it? What do you tell developers about its limits?
You escalate and the director keeps their priority. What now?
In your real example, what did you learn about writing dependency agreements?

rules.ask: What two options do you put in front of the director, with what costs, and what do you recommend?
Who owns that temporary path, how do you know when to remove it, and what if it is still there a year later?
Who reviews and runs that code after launch, and what did their team agree to?
Who has to agree to moving part of the launch, and what do developers see?
What did you personally negotiate, and what did you give up?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for privacy-preserving, on-device aggregation
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, redesign for on-device and privacy-preserving computation

angle: the data model and why it held up
the hardest correctness problem you solved
the most important reliability decision you made
privacy_feature: raw events never leaving the device, only aggregates
a per-day limit on what each device may contribute
estimates released only above a minimum population
a user's deletion reaching every derived table

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change if its inputs came from {{devices}} personal devices whose owners expect privacy, and it had to support {{privacy_feature}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes if the data came from {{devices}} personal devices and the system had to support {{privacy_feature}}: what moves onto the device, what the server may still know, what the people who use your outputs lose, and how you would show it works. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The device-based, privacy-preserving setting is hypothetical and describes general techniques, not how any company builds its systems.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; an honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible privacy redesign that places computation on the device, states what the server may still know, recognises that hashing is not anonymisation, and is honest about which outputs become estimates or are lost; a concrete, verifiable path to the privacy feature; own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a data system?
clarifications.a: It should move, store or compute data that others depend on; a service with a significant data model counts.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: Do I need to know differential privacy in depth?
clarifications.a: No. Reason from what must stay on the device, what may leave and in what form; use the terms you know correctly.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to keys, schemas, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the privacy question, start from who would be harmed if your system's raw data were exposed, and work out what the server never needs to see.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
If raw events stayed on {{devices}} devices, which of your outputs could you still compute, which would become estimates, and which would you lose?
How would you add {{privacy_feature}} without a rewrite, and how would you prove it holds?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
If the server could no longer link two events from one device, which of your tables and joins would still work?
Could someone with your table and one other public dataset re-identify a person? How do you know?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
Which of your outputs becomes too noisy to use, and what do you tell the team that relied on it?
